about.p: At advanced level, knowing a word is only half the job: you also need to know the company it keeps. We *shoulder the blame* and *foot the bill*; an argument can be *flimsy* or *watertight*; prices can *soar* or *plummet*. This course teaches the collocations that make advanced speaking and writing sound precise, natural and confident.

Units 1–6 show how collocations work and how to find, record and learn them. Units 7–11 look at metaphor, intensifying and softening adverbs, *make* and its relatives, communicating, and phrasal verbs. Units 12–45 present collocations by topic – work and study, leisure and lifestyle, the modern world and people – and units 46–60 cover basic concepts such as time, sound and change, and functions such as comparing, persuading and describing feelings.

about.-: Every card teaches a whole collocation with its meaning and an example: learn the phrase, not just the single word.
*Complete the phrase* questions hide one word of a collocation and ask you to choose it – the key skill at this level.
Many of these collocations are formal or typical of writing; notes on the cards tell you when a phrase is informal or especially formal.

about.tip: Keep a collocation notebook organised by topic, and write each new phrase into a sentence about your own life, work or studies.

units.sub: bitterly cold, take a risk, heavy rain

L.p: A *collocation* is a pair or group of words that regularly appear together. Native speakers say *bitterly cold*, *take a risk* and *heavy rain*; they don't say *bitterly hot*, *make a risk* or *thick rain*, even though no grammar rule forbids them. Choosing the expected partner makes your English sound fluent, while choosing an unexpected one – even when the meaning is clear – marks you out as a learner.

L.e: It was bitterly cold on the morning of the race. You take a risk every time you cross that road. Heavy rain is forecast for the weekend. My nephew has a keen interest in astronomy.

L.x: We *took a risk* (not *made a risk*) by putting our savings into the business.

L.h: B Why collocations matter at advanced level

L.p: At advanced level, collocation helps you to be precise. Instead of calling a problem *big*, you can call it *acute*, *pressing* or *deep-rooted*; instead of *a lot of criticism*, you can speak of *a barrage of criticism*. Collocations also let you change your style: a formal report might say that sales *rose sharply*, while a friend might say they *went through the roof*.

L.e: The housing shortage is an acute problem in the capital. The minister faced a barrage of criticism after her speech. Sales rose sharply in the final quarter. Ticket prices have gone through the roof.

L.p: Collocations are best learnt as chunks: store *a pressing need* or *strike a balance* as single items rather than as separate words. Whenever you meet a new word, *pay attention to* the words around it – the verbs, adjectives and prepositions it attracts. Over time you will *develop a feel for* which combinations sound right.

L.e: There is a pressing need for more nurses in rural areas. It's hard to strike a balance between work and family. Pay attention to the prepositions that follow adjectives. After a year in Leeds she had developed a real feel for the language.

units.sub: pitch dark, by and large, a big house

L.p: In a *strong collocation*, one word strongly predicts the other: *pitch* almost always goes with *dark* or *black*, and *ulterior* hardly ever appears without *motive*. Other strong partnerships are *shrug your shoulders*, *wreak havoc* and *inclement weather*. These are worth learning carefully because there is rarely another way of saying the same thing.

L.e: The garden was pitch dark when we got home. When I asked where he'd been, he just shrugged his shoulders. I suspect she has an ulterior motive for being so helpful. The storm wreaked havoc along the coast. Inclement weather delayed the start of the match.

L.p: A *fixed collocation* cannot be changed at all: you cannot replace, add or remove a word. Examples are *by and large* (generally), *to all intents and purposes* (in effect), *in the nick of time* (only just in time) and *few and far between* (rare). Many fixed collocations are idioms whose meaning is not obvious from the separate words.

L.e: By and large, the students were happy with the course. To all intents and purposes, the decision has already been made. We reached the station in the nick of time. Good jobs are few and far between round here.

L.x: *By and large* (not *by and long*), the new timetable has worked well.

L.p: In a *weak collocation*, a word combines with a wide range of partners: you can have *a big house*, *a big decision*, *a big mistake* and many more. Words like *good*, *big* and *have* combine almost freely. Weak collocations are easy, but advanced learners should replace them with stronger, more precise choices where possible: not just *a big mistake* but *a grave error*, not just *very angry* but *livid*.

L.e: Moving abroad was a big decision for the whole family. It was a grave error to ignore the warnings. My father was livid when he saw the dent in the car.

units.sub: adjective + noun, verb + adverb, noun + of + noun

L.p: The commonest type is *adjective + noun*: *a chequered history*, *a fleeting glimpse*, *a sweeping statement*. Nouns also combine with other nouns, as in *a pang of guilt* (noun + *of* + noun), and with verbs, either as the subject (*rumours circulate*) or as the object (*meet a deadline*, *launch a campaign*).

L.e: The club has a chequered history, with many ups and downs. I caught a fleeting glimpse of her as the train pulled out. It's a sweeping statement to say that all teenagers are lazy. I felt a pang of guilt when I saw the uneaten cake. Rumours are circulating that the factory will close. We worked all weekend to meet the deadline.

L.p: Verbs combine with adverbs (*deeply regret*, *flatly refuse*) and with prepositional phrases (*fall into disrepair*, *burst into tears*). Adjectives combine with adverbs (*utterly exhausted*, *highly controversial*) and are often followed by a particular preposition (*fraught with danger*, *riddled with errors*).

L.e: I deeply regret what I said to you. The old cinema has fallen into disrepair. After the climb we were utterly exhausted. The essay was riddled with spelling errors. The crossing was fraught with danger.

L.x: The report was *riddled with* (not *riddled of*) mistakes.

L.p: Some collocations are longer patterns: verb + noun + preposition (*take pride in*, *take advantage of*), verb + adjective (*fall silent*, *run dry*, *go missing*) and *binomials* – pairs joined by *and* in a fixed order, such as *peace and quiet* or *safe and sound*.

L.e: She takes great pride in her garden. The room fell silent when he walked in. The wells ran dry during the drought. All I want this weekend is some peace and quiet. The children got home safe and sound.

units.sub: look up a word, consult a dictionary, search a corpus

L.p: A good learner's dictionary does more than define a word: it shows the words it typically combines with, often in bold type or in the example sentences. When you *look up a word*, read the examples as carefully as the definition. A *collocations dictionary* lists the verbs, adjectives and nouns that go with each headword, so it is the best place to check whether a noun goes with *make* or *take*. In formal English you *consult a dictionary*.

L.e: If you're not sure of a phrase, look it up. Many writers consult a dictionary of collocations when drafting. I checked the expression in an online dictionary before putting it in my essay.

L.x: I *looked the word up* (not *searched the word*) in my dictionary.

L.p: A *corpus* is a large collection of real texts stored on a computer. Searching a corpus shows you which words *occur together* most often, in which kinds of text and in which order; the results appear as *concordance lines*, with the key word in the middle of each line. Even a simple internet search can help you *compare frequencies* – but remember that not everything online is good English.

L.e: The corpus shows that 'heavy traffic' is far more common than 'strong traffic'. Concordance lines let you see a word in dozens of real contexts. Before using a new phrase, I compare frequencies with a quick search.

L.p: Collocations are everywhere in *authentic material*: newspapers, podcasts, lectures and novels. *Make a note of* useful phrases as you read, *draw up a list* of key collocations for each topic you study, and *test yourself* regularly. A thesaurus can help you find a more precise word, but always check how that word combines before you use it.

L.e: Authentic material lets you meet collocations in context. I've drawn up a list of collocations for my business course. Make a note of any phrase that surprises you.

units.sub: notice patterns, record collocations, keep a notebook

L.h: A Noticing collocations as you read

L.p: Reading is the richest source of collocations, but only if you *read actively*. As you read, *notice patterns*: which adjectives a noun attracts, which verbs come before it and which prepositions follow it. Highlighting whole phrases rather than single words *trains your eye* to see language in chunks.

L.e: Reading actively means stopping to think about how a phrase is built. I've started to notice patterns in the way journalists describe the economy. Underlining whole phrases has trained my eye to spot collocations.

L.p: *Keep a notebook*, on paper or on your phone, and *record collocations* in a way that suits you: by topic, by key word, or in *word forks* – a key word with its partners branching out from it. *Jot down* the sentence in which you met the phrase, so that you remember its context, and add a note on register: formal, informal or technical.

L.e: I keep a notebook just for collocations. My sister records collocations by topic: health, money, travel. Jot down the whole sentence, not just the phrase. Draw a word fork for 'decision' with all the verbs that go with it.

L.h: C Working on what you have recorded

L.p: Recording is only the first step. *Revise regularly* (in British English, *revise* means study again), *put the phrases into practice* in your own speaking and writing, and *recycle* them in new contexts. A useful exercise is to rewrite a paragraph using stronger collocations, or to cover one word of each pair and *test your memory*.

L.e: Revise your notebook regularly – a little every day works best. Try to put new phrases into practice in the same week you meet them. I rewrote my introduction using stronger collocations. Cover the verbs and test your memory.

units.t: Finding and working on collocations in texts

units.sub: lodge a complaint, have a go, pay a visit

L.p: Collocations, like single words, belong to different *registers*. In formal writing you *lodge a complaint* and *make an inquiry*; in conversation you have a moan and ask around. Many informal collocations use simple verbs such as *have*, *get* and *give*: *have a go* (try), *give someone a ring* (phone them), *get the hang of* something (learn how to do it).

L.e: Residents have lodged a formal complaint with the council. Let me have a go at fixing it. I'll give you a ring tomorrow evening. It took me weeks to get the hang of the new software.

L.x: I'll *give you a ring* (not *make you a ring*) after work.

L.p: Every profession has its own collocations. Lawyers *file a lawsuit* and judges *dismiss a case*; doctors *prescribe medication* and nurses *administer a drug*; scientists *conduct an experiment* and *collect data*. Using the right verb for the field shows that you know the subject, so learn the collocations of your own area of work or study.

L.e: The family filed a lawsuit against the builders. The judge dismissed the case for lack of evidence. The nurse administered the drug through a drip. The team conducted a series of experiments on bees.

L.p: Mixing registers sounds odd: a business email should not ask a colleague to *have a go* at a report, and a text to a friend should not announce that you will *pay a visit* to their flat – *pop round* is far more natural. Some collocations are neutral and fit anywhere, such as *take part* or *make a decision*. *Pay someone a visit* is slightly formal or humorous; *drop in on someone* is informal.

L.e: The inspector will pay us a visit next week. Pop round for a coffee whenever you like. Do drop in on us if you're ever in York. Over two hundred people took part in the survey.

units.sub: foot the bill, heavy burden, run into trouble

L.p: A metaphor uses a word in a non-literal way, and many common collocations are metaphors based on the human body. You *face the facts* when you accept an unpleasant truth, *shoulder the blame* when you accept responsibility for something bad, and *foot the bill* when you pay. A person can *head a team* (lead it), *have an eye for* detail or beauty (be good at noticing it) and *keep others on their toes* (make them stay alert). Things that occur together *go hand in hand*.

L.e: We have to face the facts: the shop is losing money. The captain shouldered the blame for the defeat. Guess who footed the bill for the party? Dr Patel heads a team of six researchers. A good editor has an eye for detail. Surprise inspections keep the staff on their toes. Poverty and poor health often go hand in hand.

L.x: She *has an eye for* (not *has an eye on*) colour, so ask her to choose the paint.

L.h: B Metaphors of weight and size

L.p: Weight words often describe seriousness. A *heavy burden* or a *heavy responsibility* is hard to carry, and *weighty matters* are serious and important. The opposite, *light*, suggests something that is not serious: *light reading* is easy, enjoyable reading. Size words describe chances: a *slim chance* is small but real, while *fat chance* (informal and ironic) means almost none. When a worry ends, it is *a weight off your mind*.

L.e: Caring for her sick father was a heavy burden. The committee has weighty matters to discuss today. I only take light reading on holiday. There's a slim chance the flight will leave on time. 'Will he pay you back?' 'Fat chance!' Selling the house was a weight off my mind.

L.h: C Metaphors of movement and journeys

L.p: Life is often described as a journey. People *run into trouble* or *run into difficulties*; a plan or a relationship can *hit the rocks* – fail, like a ship that crashes – and is then *on the rocks*. Someone who passes a test easily *sails through* it. If you avoid something, you *steer clear of* it, and at a moment of important choice you are *at a crossroads*.

L.e: The project ran into difficulties in its second year. Their marriage hit the rocks soon after the move. She sailed through her driving test. I try to steer clear of arguments about politics. At forty, he felt he was at a crossroads in his career.

units.sub: deeply offensive, spotlessly clean, wildly inaccurate

L.p: Advanced speakers rarely just say *very*. Different adverbs prefer different partners: a remark is *deeply offensive*, a kitchen *spotlessly clean*, a guess *wildly inaccurate*, a plan *fundamentally flawed*. Some adverbs mean 'completely' and go with extreme adjectives: *utterly ridiculous*, *totally unacceptable*, *absolutely furious*.

L.e: Some of his jokes were deeply offensive. Her flat is always spotlessly clean. The early estimates turned out to be wildly inaccurate. The scheme is fundamentally flawed and should be scrapped. That idea is utterly ridiculous.

L.x: The bathroom was *spotlessly clean* (not *spotlessly tidy*) when we arrived.

L.p: Verbs have favourite adverbs too. You *strongly recommend*, *firmly believe*, *sincerely hope* and *bitterly regret*; you *categorically refuse* or *flatly deny*. Some adverbs usually go before the verb (*I fully understand*) and some after it (*she laughed heartily*, *he slept soundly*).

L.e: I strongly recommend booking in advance. We sincerely hope you enjoy your stay. He bitterly regretted leaving school at sixteen. I fully understand your concerns. The baby slept soundly all night.

L.p: Softening adverbs make a statement less strong, which is often more polite or more accurate. You can be *slightly concerned*, *somewhat surprised* or *mildly amused*; a film can be *loosely based* on real events, and one plan *broadly similar* to another. In formal writing, *relatively*, *fairly* and *reasonably* are useful: *a relatively small number*, *reasonably priced*.

L.e: I was slightly concerned when she didn't reply. The audience seemed mildly amused by the speech. The series is loosely based on a true story. The two proposals are broadly similar. The hotel was clean and reasonably priced.

units.sub: make a contribution, make a habit of, turn in a profit

L.p: *Make* forms dozens of collocations with nouns. You *make a contribution* (give money, help or ideas), *make a habit of* doing something (do it regularly), *make allowances for* someone (be less strict because of their situation), *make amends* (do something to put a wrong right), *make a point of* doing something (do it deliberately because it matters to you) and *make your mark* (become known for something). Notice also *make sense of* (understand) and *make the most of* (use fully).

L.e: Everyone made a contribution to the leaving present. Don't make a habit of arriving late. The teacher made allowances for his illness. She brought flowers to make amends for forgetting my birthday. I make a point of reading the small print. The young designer quickly made her mark in Milan. It took me a while to make sense of the instructions.

L.x: Try to *make the most of* (not *do the most of*) your time in London.

L.p: Several verbs mean *make* or *produce* in particular contexts. A company *turns in a profit* or *generates income*; an event *creates a stir* (causes excitement); a writer *churns out* books (produces a lot of them quickly, often without much care). Talks *yield results*, a factory *manufactures goods* and a cook *whips up* a meal (makes it quickly).

L.e: Despite the recession, the firm turned in a healthy profit. The new visitor centre will generate income for the town. Her outfit created quite a stir at the premiere. He churns out a thriller every six months. The talks have yet to yield any results. She whipped up a delicious omelette in five minutes.

L.p: Learners often confuse *make* and *do*. As a rough guide, *do* is used for tasks and activities (*do the housework*, *do business*, *do someone a favour*, *do damage*), while *make* is used for creating or producing (*make a mess*, *make progress*, *make an exception*, *make a fortune*). Many of these collocations simply have to be learnt.

L.e: Could you do me a favour and post this letter? The storm did a lot of damage to the roof. We're making good progress with the new website. I don't usually lend money, but I'll make an exception for you. He made a fortune selling software.

L.x: The flood *did* (not *made*) serious damage to the library.

units.sub: generally speaking, talk business, get a message across

L.p: Many collocations with *speak* are fixed phrases that introduce a point of view: *generally speaking*, *strictly speaking* (to be exact), *broadly speaking* and *personally speaking*. You *speak your mind* when you say honestly what you think, and you *speak highly of* someone when you praise them. With *talk*, you *talk business* (discuss work or a deal), *talk sense* or *talk nonsense*, and *talk shop* (discuss work at a social occasion, often annoyingly).

L.e: Generally speaking, the trains here are reliable. Strictly speaking, the museum closes at five, but the guards usually let you stay a little longer. She always speaks her mind, even to the boss. Your old teacher speaks very highly of you. Let's have lunch first and talk business afterwards. Please don't talk shop at the dinner table.

L.x: Her teachers *speak highly of* (not *talk highly of*) her.

L.p: When you communicate successfully, you *get your message across* or *get your point across*. You *convey a message*, *express an opinion* or, formally, *voice concerns*. If you want many people to know something, you *spread the word*; when you *break the news*, you tell someone something unwelcome. Something said indirectly *drops a hint*, and the listener *takes the hint* if they understand it.

L.e: The campaign got its message across very effectively. Several parents voiced concerns about the new timetable. Can you spread the word that the meeting has moved? It fell to me to break the news to the team. I dropped a few hints about what I wanted for my birthday, but he didn't take the hint.

L.p: Communication can *break down* (fail), and people can *get the wrong end of the stick* (misunderstand completely, informal) or *talk at cross purposes* (discuss different things without realising it). Jokes get *lost in translation*, and advice can *fall on deaf ears* (be ignored). You *clear up a misunderstanding* when you explain what you really meant.

L.e: Communication between the two departments has broken down. I think you've got the wrong end of the stick – I wasn't criticising you. We were talking at cross purposes for ten minutes. Some of the humour was lost in translation. My warnings fell on deaf ears. A quick phone call cleared up the misunderstanding.

units.sub: take up office, work up an appetite, see off an intruder

L.h: A Phrasal verbs with typical objects

L.p: Many phrasal verbs have favourite objects. A politician *takes up office* (starts an official job); you *work up an appetite* (become hungry through activity) or *work up the courage* to do something. A guard dog *sees off an intruder* (chases them away). You *run up a bill* or *run up debts* (let them grow), *put forward a proposal*, *carry out research*, *draw up a contract* and *call off a strike*.

L.e: The new mayor takes up office in May. A long walk on the beach always works up an appetite. It took me a week to work up the courage to ask her. Our neighbour's dog saw off a burglar last night. They ran up a huge phone bill while travelling. The union called off the strike at the last minute.

L.x: The council *carried out* (not *made out*) a survey of local businesses.

L.h: B Phrasal verbs with typical subjects

L.p: Other phrasal verbs are typically used with particular subjects. *War breaks out*, and so do fires, fights and epidemics. *Talks break down*; *the weather clears up*; *a problem crops up* (appears unexpectedly). *Prices shoot up* (rise very quickly) and *supplies run out*. *A new idea catches on* when it becomes popular.

L.e: War broke out in 1939. Fighting broke out between rival fans. Talks between the two sides have broken down. Something's cropped up at work, so I'll be late. House prices have shot up this year. Our water ran out on the third day. The fashion caught on very quickly.

L.p: Many phrasal verbs have related nouns that form their own collocations: a *breakdown in communications*, a *breakthrough in research*, *cutbacks in spending*, a *setback to a plan*, a *high turnout* at an election, a *shake-up* of the management, a *takeover bid*. These nouns are common in journalism and formal writing.

L.e: There has been a major breakthrough in cancer research. The hospital faces severe cutbacks. Bad weather was a serious setback to the rescue. Turnout at the election was very low. The new director announced a shake-up of the sales team.

units.sub: make a living, take up a post, move up the ladder

L.p: You *make a living* or *earn a living* from your work; if you only just have enough money, you *scrape a living*. A job can be *well paid* or *badly paid*, *full-time* or *part-time*, *permanent* or *temporary*, and many people now *do freelance work* or *work flexible hours*. If you have several jobs or duties at once, you *juggle* them.

L.e: My cousin makes a living as a wedding photographer. Many artists scrape a living from teaching. Nurses are badly paid for such responsible work. I do freelance work for three magazines. My contract lets me work flexible hours. He juggles two part-time jobs.

L.x: He *earns a living* (not *wins a living*) as a taxi driver.

L.p: In formal English, you *take up a post* or *take up a position* when you start a job, and you *hold a post* while you are in it. You *apply for a vacancy* and, when you decide to leave, *hand in your notice*. If your job is no longer needed, you *are made redundant*; some people *take early retirement*.

L.e: Dr Lee will take up her post as head of department in September. He has held the post for over a decade. I handed in my notice on Friday. Two hundred workers were made redundant when the factory closed. My uncle took early retirement at fifty-five.

L.p: Success at work is often described as climbing: you *move up the ladder*, *climb the career ladder* or *work your way up* from a junior job. You *gain promotion*, *take on responsibility* and *build a career*. If your career stops progressing, you *reach a plateau*, and if an unofficial barrier stops you rising, you *hit a glass ceiling*.

L.e: She worked her way up from receptionist to managing director. He moved quickly up the ladder at the bank. I'm ready to take on more responsibility. After ten years she felt she had reached a plateau. Many women still hit a glass ceiling in the law.

units.sub: fit the job description, land a new job, menial tasks

L.p: When a company *advertises a vacancy*, you apply by sending a *covering letter* (British English) with your CV. Check first that you *fit the job description* and *meet the criteria*. Employers then *draw up a shortlist* of the strongest candidates; if you get through that stage, you *are shortlisted* and invited to an interview.

L.e: The library is advertising a vacancy for an assistant. Keep your covering letter short and clear. I don't quite fit the job description – they want five years' experience. Only applicants who meet the criteria will be contacted. Six of us were shortlisted for the post.

L.x: Applicants must *meet the criteria* (not *fill the criteria*) set out in the advert.

L.p: When you are offered work after a long search, you *land a job* (informal) or *secure a position* (formal). A job can be a *dream job*, a *dead-end job* (with no prospects) or a *stopgap* – something temporary until a better job comes along. Many contracts begin with a *probationary period*, a trial period during which either side can end the arrangement easily.

L.e: After months of searching, she landed a job with a design agency. He secured a position at the embassy. It's not my dream job, but it pays the bills. I don't want to get stuck in a dead-end job. Bar work was only a stopgap while I studied. New staff serve a three-month probationary period.

L.p: In a new job you *learn the ropes* (learn how things are done) and may be given *menial tasks* (boring, unskilled jobs) at first; a colleague who teaches you *shows you the ropes*. Gradually you *find your feet* and are expected to *pull your weight* (do your fair share). If you are given difficult work with no preparation, you are *thrown in at the deep end*.

L.e: It took me a few weeks to learn the ropes. Interns often complain about being given menial tasks. Kate will show you the ropes on your first day. She soon found her feet and was running projects of her own. Everyone in a small team has to pull their weight. I was thrown in at the deep end on my first morning.

units.sub: bear in mind, widespread belief, jump to conclusions

L.p: You *bear something in mind* when you remember it while making a decision. If you *give something some thought* or *give it careful consideration*, you think about it seriously. An idea can *cross your mind* (occur to you briefly) or *spring to mind* (come quickly). When you are trying very hard to remember or solve something, you *rack your brains*.

L.e: Bear in mind that the shops close early on Sundays. I've given your offer some thought, and I accept. It never crossed my mind that she might be lonely. When I think of summer, cricket springs to mind. I racked my brains, but I couldn't remember his name.

L.x: *Bear in mind* (not *carry in mind*) that all forms must be signed.

L.p: A *widespread belief* is held by many people; a *firm belief* is held strongly. Research can *challenge a belief* or *dispel a myth*. An idea can be *bright*, *novel* (new and original), *half-baked* (not properly thought out) or *far-fetched* (hard to believe). You *toy with an idea* when you consider it, but not very seriously.

L.e: Contrary to widespread belief, bats are not blind. It is my firm belief that every child should learn to swim. The study challenges the belief that money makes us happy. Selling soup at the station was a novel idea. That's a half-baked idea – you haven't thought about the costs. I'm toying with the idea of learning Greek.

L.p: You *come to a conclusion* or *reach a conclusion* after careful thought; if you decide too quickly, without the facts, you *jump to conclusions*. A *foregone conclusion* is a result that is certain from the start. You *draw a conclusion* from evidence. If there is no doubt at all about something, it is *beyond question*.

L.e: After weeks of discussion, the committee reached a conclusion. Don't jump to conclusions – there may be a simple explanation. The result of the vote was a foregone conclusion. What conclusions can we draw from the data? Her honesty is beyond question.

units.sub: fierce competition, stimulate growth, hike in prices

L.p: Business reports describe *fierce competition*, *stiff competition* or *cut-throat competition* (very aggressive). Companies *gain a foothold* in a market (win a first, small position), *corner the market* (control it) or *lose ground* to their rivals. A firm with no serious rivals *dominates the market*.

L.e: There is fierce competition between the two supermarket chains. The airline faces stiff competition on its European routes. The company has gained a foothold in the Asian market. Local shops are losing ground to online retailers. One firm dominates the market for search engines.

L.x: The company faces *stiff competition* (not *hard competition*) from cheaper brands.

L.p: Governments try to *stimulate growth* or *boost the economy*, and firms aim for *sustained growth* – growth that continues over years. Figures can show *a steady increase*, *a sharp rise* or *a dramatic fall*. A sudden increase in prices or taxes, especially in newspapers, is a *hike in prices* or *a tax hike*. When business gets worse, a company *suffers a downturn*; when it improves again, there is *an upturn*.

L.e: Lower interest rates should stimulate growth. The firm has achieved ten years of sustained growth. There was a sharp rise in sales in December. Passengers are angry about the latest hike in fares. The industry suffered a downturn after the crisis. Analysts expect an upturn next year.

L.p: Companies *publish annual results*, *announce record profits* or *report losses*. They *exceed their targets* or *fall short of expectations*. *Profits soar* or *plummet*, while *costs spiral* (rise out of control). A cautious forecast might speak of *a modest increase* or *a slight dip*.

L.e: The bank announced record profits this morning. Sales exceeded our targets for the third year running. Second-quarter results fell short of expectations. Profits plummeted after the scandal. Energy costs have spiralled. The report predicts a modest increase in demand.

units.sub: fit for purpose, kick up a fuss, grounds for complaint

L.p: Goods should be *fit for purpose* – able to do the job they are sold for. If they are not, you are usually *entitled to a refund* or a replacement. Keep your receipt as *proof of purchase*; a product that is *under guarantee* will be repaired free for a certain time. Instead of cash, some shops offer a *credit note* to spend in the store.

L.e: A raincoat that lets in water is hardly fit for purpose. You're entitled to a refund if the item is faulty. Please bring your receipt as proof of purchase. The washing machine is still under guarantee. They wouldn't give me my money back, only a credit note.

L.x: The kettle is still *under guarantee* (not *in guarantee*), so they'll repair it.

L.p: If you are unhappy, you *make a complaint*, *lodge a complaint* (formal) or, in conversation, *kick up a fuss* (complain loudly). You need *grounds for complaint* – good reasons. A *legitimate complaint* is fair and reasonable; a *trivial complaint* is about something unimportant. Companies *handle* or *resolve complaints*, and after a disaster they may receive *a flood of complaints*.

L.e: I had to kick up a fuss before they agreed to change the room. If the train was three hours late, you certainly have grounds for complaint. The manager agreed that it was a legitimate complaint. The council received a flood of complaints about the noise. Our team resolves most complaints within a week.

L.p: Service can be *prompt* and *courteous*, or *shoddy* (poor) and *sloppy*. Good companies *go the extra mile* (make a special effort), *put things right* when they go wrong and win *customer loyalty*. Bad experiences can *damage a company's reputation*, and an apology may come with *a goodwill gesture* such as a voucher.

L.e: The hotel staff were courteous and prompt. The builders did a shoddy job on the roof. That shop always goes the extra mile for its customers. They apologised and offered a free meal as a goodwill gesture. One bad review can damage a firm's reputation.

units.sub: gifted child, mature student, thirst for knowledge

L.p: A *gifted child* has unusual ability, and schools may run special programmes for *high achievers*. A *mature student* (British English) starts university later than usual, often after some years at work. Students who are eager to learn have *a thirst for knowledge* or *an inquiring mind*.

L.e: Gifted children sometimes get bored in ordinary classes. The school runs a summer programme for high achievers. As a mature student, I found the reading easier than the late nights. Even at eighty, my grandfather has a real thirst for knowledge. Good teachers encourage an inquiring mind.

L.x: My aunt went to university as a *mature student* (not *old student*) at forty.

L.p: At university you *attend lectures*, *take notes* and *hand in assignments* by the deadline. Before exams you *revise* (British English) or *cram* – study a great deal in a short time. You *sit an exam* or *take an exam*, and then *pass with flying colours* (very successfully), *scrape through* (only just pass) or *fail*. In Britain you can often *resit* an exam that you failed.

L.e: I try to attend every lecture, even the early ones. She crammed for her chemistry exam all weekend. We sit our finals in June. He passed his driving test with flying colours. I only just scraped through maths. You can resit the paper in August.

L.x: She *passed* (not *succeeded*) all her exams with flying colours.

L.p: Students *enrol on a course* (British English); in formal British English they *read* a subject, as in *read law*. Many *take out a student loan* and *live in halls of residence* in their first year. At the end they *graduate*, perhaps with *a first-class degree* – the highest grade in Britain – and some *go on to postgraduate study*.

L.e: I've enrolled on an evening course in Italian. He read history at Edinburgh. Most first-year students live in halls of residence. She graduated with a first-class degree in physics. Many students take out a loan to cover their fees.

units.sub: working hypothesis, confront issues, critical analysis

L.p: Academic writing starts with a question. You *formulate a hypothesis* or begin with a *working hypothesis* – an idea to test, which may change as you go. You *carry out a survey*, *collect data* and *consult sources*. A good writer *narrows down the topic*, *draws on* earlier studies and acknowledges the work of others.

L.e: Our working hypothesis was that sleep affects memory. We carried out a survey of two hundred commuters. She drew on several earlier studies. Every source you consult must appear in the bibliography. I need to narrow down my topic – it's far too broad.

L.p: In the body of an essay, you *put forward an argument*, *support it with evidence* and *cite examples*. You *confront issues* – deal with difficult questions directly – rather than avoiding them, and you *address counter-arguments*. A *critical analysis* examines strengths and weaknesses; a *balanced view* considers both sides.

L.e: The author puts forward a convincing argument for reform. Support each claim with evidence from the reading. A good essay confronts the issues head on. Address the counter-arguments before you conclude. The assignment asks for a critical analysis of the policy. Try to present a balanced view.

L.x: Each paragraph should *put forward* (not *put on*) one clear argument.

L.p: In your conclusion, you *sum up the main points*, *draw conclusions* and perhaps *make recommendations*. Findings may *shed light on* a problem (help to explain it) or *pave the way for* further research. Before you submit your work, proofread it carefully and check that it *meets the word limit*.

L.e: The final section sums up the main points. The report makes three recommendations to the council. These findings shed light on why some children struggle to read. Her study paved the way for new treatments. Always proofread before you submit an assignment. My essay was well over the word limit.

units.sub: call for a celebration, social whirl, play host to

L.p: Good news *calls for a celebration*. You *throw a party*, send out invitations and look after your guests; in formal English, a city *plays host to* an event when it takes place there. A busy period full of social events is a *social whirl*. In British English you *have people round* when you invite them to your home.

L.e: You've passed your driving test? That calls for a celebration! We're throwing a party for Ben's fortieth. Edinburgh plays host to a huge arts festival every August. December is a social whirl of dinners and drinks. We often have friends round on Saturday evenings.

L.x: Let's *throw a party* (not *make a party*) when the exams are over.

L.p: At social events you *strike up a conversation* with strangers and *make small talk* (polite conversation about unimportant things). If you *hit it off* with someone, you like each other immediately. You keep in touch with some friends and *lose touch* with others. People who prefer their own company *keep themselves to themselves*.

L.e: I struck up a conversation with the man next to me on the train. I'm hopeless at making small talk at weddings. We hit it off the moment we met. I lost touch with most of my school friends. Our new neighbours keep themselves to themselves.

L.p: In formal English you *extend an invitation*; the guest accepts it or *declines the invitation*, perhaps because of a *prior engagement* (an earlier arrangement). Hosts *lay on* food and drink (provide it, often generously), and a guest who stays too long *outstays their welcome*.

L.e: The ambassador extended an invitation to all the visiting students. I'm afraid I must decline the invitation owing to a prior engagement. Our hosts laid on a magnificent buffet. We left at ten – we didn't want to outstay our welcome.

units.sub: juicy gossip, broach the subject, opening gambit

L.p: Informal talk can be a *chat*, a *natter* (British English, informal) or *idle chatter* – talk about nothing important. *Juicy gossip* is interesting, often shocking news about other people's private lives; you *catch up on the gossip* with friends. Something said *in confidence* is meant to stay secret, and you *break a confidence* if you repeat it.

L.e: We had a good natter over coffee. I'm tired of idle chatter about celebrities. Have you heard the latest juicy gossip about the boss? Come round and catch up on all the gossip. I told you that in confidence – please don't pass it on.

L.x: We *had a chat* (not *made a chat*) about the holidays.

L.h: B Starting and steering a conversation

L.p: You *broach a subject* when you raise a difficult or sensitive topic. An *opening gambit* is a first remark planned to start things off or to gain an advantage. A speaker who avoids the main point *beats about the bush*; one who doesn't *comes straight to the point*. When nobody knows what to say, there is *an awkward silence*.

L.e: I didn't know how to broach the subject of money with my parents. His opening gambit was to praise the chairman's tie. Stop beating about the bush and tell me what's wrong. She came straight to the point: she wanted a pay rise. There was an awkward silence after his joke.

L.p: A conversation can turn into a *heated discussion* or a *blazing row* (British English, a very angry argument). You *have words with* someone when you speak to them angrily about a problem, and you *have a bone to pick with* someone when you want to complain about something they did. Afterwards you *clear the air* by talking honestly.

L.e: The meeting turned into a heated discussion about parking. They had a blazing row in the middle of the restaurant. I'll have words with him about his timekeeping. I've got a bone to pick with you – you ate my lunch! We went for a walk to clear the air.

units.sub: declare independence, reach agreement, bow to pressure

L.p: News reports are full of fixed partnerships. A country *declares independence*, holds elections or *imposes sanctions* on another state. Leaders *hold talks* and, if all goes well, *reach agreement*. A party or leader *comes to power* and may later *cling to power* (try desperately to keep it). A leader who *bows to pressure* changes a decision because people demand it.

L.e: The island declared independence in 1964. The two leaders held talks in Geneva. After months of negotiation, they reached agreement on fishing rights. The general came to power in a coup. The minister finally bowed to pressure and resigned.

L.x: The two sides *reached agreement* (not *arrived to agreement*) late last night.

L.p: Disasters *strike*: an earthquake strikes a region, floods sweep through towns and *fires rage* out of control. Emergency services launch a rescue operation and *evacuate residents*. Governments *declare a state of emergency* and send in aid, while *the death toll rises* as news comes in.

L.e: A powerful earthquake struck the region early this morning. Forest fires have been raging for a week. Police evacuated residents from the low-lying streets. The government has declared a state of emergency. The death toll has risen to more than two hundred.

L.p: Stories *hit the headlines*; a big *story breaks* (becomes public for the first time) and journalists cover it. Newspapers *run a story* (publish it) and may issue a correction if they get something wrong. A source who does not want to be named speaks *on condition of anonymity*.

L.e: The scandal hit the headlines last week. The story broke on Sunday evening. Three reporters covered the trial. An official, speaking on condition of anonymity, confirmed the plans. The paper ran the story on its front page.

units.sub: refuse point-blank, decline to comment, gauge reaction

L.p: Public figures under pressure often *decline to comment*. They may *refuse point-blank* (refuse completely and directly) to answer, *sidestep a question* (avoid it skilfully) or give a *non-committal answer* – one that doesn't show what they think. When they are ready, they *issue a statement*, sometimes after a leak has already revealed the story.

L.e: The minister declined to comment on the rumours. She refused point-blank to discuss her private life. He skilfully sidestepped the question about taxes. When pressed, she gave a non-committal answer. The company issued a statement this afternoon.

L.p: Politicians try to *gauge reaction* (judge how people feel) before acting, often by commissioning a poll. Policies can *spark protests*, provoke an outcry or win public support. *Public opinion* can swing behind or against a leader, and *support* can *wane* (gradually decrease). An unpopular decision may lead to a *backlash*.

L.e: The party published the plan early to gauge reaction. The proposal sparked protests in several cities. Public opinion has swung against the war. Support for the government is waning. There was a fierce backlash against the new parking charges.

L.x: The new law *sparked protests* (not *fired protests*) across the country.

L.p: Politicians become *embroiled in a scandal* (deeply involved in it), face *calls to resign* and sometimes step down. Opponents *demand an inquiry*, and the government may set one up. An affair can *rock the government* (shock and weaken it), but a leader who survives *weathers the storm*.

L.e: The health minister became embroiled in a scandal over expenses. He faces growing calls to resign. Opposition leaders have demanded a public inquiry. The scandal rocked the government. Somehow the prime minister weathered the storm.

units.sub: date back to, movable feast, propose a toast

L.p: Many festivals *date back to* ancient times or *have their origins in* religious or farming customs. Communities *observe a tradition* or keep a custom alive. A *movable feast* is a festival whose date changes each year, such as Easter; informally, the phrase also describes anything with no fixed time. Some customs *die out*, while others are revived.

L.e: The fair dates back to the thirteenth century. Many harvest festivals have their origins in pagan rituals. Our village still observes the tradition of dancing round the maypole. Easter is a movable feast. Lunch in our office is a movable feast – nobody eats at the same time. The custom almost died out but was revived in the 1970s.

L.x: The festival *dates back to* (not *dates back from*) Roman times.

L.p: People celebrate an occasion, *mark an anniversary* (do something special to show its importance) and *commemorate* an event or a person (formally remember them). Celebrations can be lavish or *low-key* (quiet and simple). Crowds *line the streets* for a procession, and big festivals *draw crowds* from far away.

L.e: The town held a concert to mark the anniversary of the bridge. A statue was unveiled to commemorate the poet. It was a low-key wedding with just twenty guests. Thousands lined the streets to watch the parade. The carnival draws huge crowds every year.

L.p: At a formal dinner, someone *proposes a toast*, inviting everyone to *raise their glasses* and *drink to* someone's health or success. A good party can go on *into the small hours* (the early hours of the morning). A *surprise party* is one the guest of honour knows nothing about.

L.e: At the end of the meal, my uncle stood up to propose a toast to the newly-weds. Everyone raised their glasses to the departing headteacher. Let's drink to our new business! The celebrations went on into the small hours. We're planning a surprise party for Dad's sixtieth.

units.sub: set the trend, fashion victim, flawless complexion

L.p: Companies *launch a campaign* to *raise awareness* of a product or to *boost sales*. Adverts *target a market* (aim at a particular group of customers) and try to build a brand image. A *catchy slogan* is easy to remember. Some adverts succeed brilliantly; others *backfire* – they have the opposite effect to the one intended.

L.e: The company launched a national advertising campaign in March. The posters aim to raise awareness of heart disease. The new range targets the teenage market. Everyone remembers a catchy slogan. Their attempt at humour backfired badly.

L.x: The posters were designed to *raise awareness* (not *rise awareness*) of the problem.

L.p: Designers *set the trend* and others follow it. Clothes *come into fashion*, become *the height of fashion* and later go out of fashion. Someone who follows every fashion without asking whether it suits them is a *fashion victim*, while a *fashion statement* is a style chosen to show something about yourself.

L.e: Young designers from Seoul are setting the trend in streetwear. Wide trousers have come back into fashion. In the 1980s, shoulder pads were the height of fashion. He's a real fashion victim – he even wears sunglasses indoors. Her bright red boots made quite a fashion statement.

L.p: Advertisements for cosmetics promise *a flawless complexion* (perfect skin) and glossy hair, and claim to reduce the signs of ageing. Models *strike a pose* for the camera, and a person can look *immaculately groomed* (perfectly neat). Critics say such adverts create *unrealistic expectations*.

L.e: The cream claims to give you a flawless complexion in seven days. Shampoo adverts always show glossy hair blowing in the wind. The models struck a pose for the photographers. Even after a long flight, she looked immaculately groomed. Ads like these create unrealistic expectations among teenagers.

units.sub: lengthy delays, grind the gears, bear left

L.p: Travel reports warn of *lengthy delays*, *heavy traffic* and *tailbacks* (long queues of stopped vehicles, British English). Traffic can be *bumper to bumper* or *at a standstill*; at busy times there is *gridlock*, when nothing can move at all. Roadworks *cause disruption*, and drivers are advised to *find an alternative route* or *avoid the area*.

L.e: Motorists face lengthy delays on the coast road this weekend. There's a five-mile tailback after an accident near the junction. Traffic was bumper to bumper all the way into town. A burst water main brought the city centre to a standstill. Drivers should find an alternative route while the bridge is closed.

L.x: We were stuck in *heavy traffic* (not *big traffic*) for an hour.

L.p: Learner drivers *stall the engine* (stop it by mistake) and *grind the gears* (change gear badly, making a noise). A driver can *pull out* (move into the traffic), *pull over* (stop at the side of the road), *overtake* another car and *keep within the speed limit*. Someone who drives too close to the car in front is *tailgating*, and a driver who becomes violently angry is showing *road rage*.

L.e: On my first lesson I stalled the engine at every junction. You could hear him grinding the gears all the way up the hill. The police signalled to me to pull over. Never overtake on a bend. A lorry was tailgating us for miles. The fight was a case of road rage.

L.p: When giving directions, you *bear left* or *bear right* (follow the road gently in that direction), *take the second exit* at a roundabout and *go straight on* at the lights. Drivers *give way* to traffic on a main road, and you can *get a parking ticket*, *get points on your licence* or even *be banned from driving* for breaking the rules.

L.e: Bear left at the fork and the farm is on your right. At the roundabout, take the second exit. Go straight on at the traffic lights. Give way to traffic coming from the right. I got a parking ticket outside the hospital. He was banned from driving for a year.

units.sub: get itchy feet, off the beaten track, leg of the journey

L.p: When you feel a strong desire to travel, you *get itchy feet* (informal). Some people have *a sense of adventure* and want to *see the world*; others are happy to *broaden their horizons* (learn about new things) closer to home. Young people often *take a gap year* (British English) between school and university, and some *go backpacking* round a continent.

L.e: After two years in the same office, I'm getting itchy feet. You need a real sense of adventure to cycle across Africa. Living abroad really broadened my horizons. My brother took a gap year and worked in Peru. We went backpacking round South-East Asia.

L.x: She *took a gap year* (not *made a gap year*) before starting university.

L.p: Adventurous travellers like to go *off the beaten track* – to places few tourists visit. A place can be *remote*, *unspoilt* or *breathtakingly beautiful*. A long trip is divided into *legs*; on *the final leg of the journey* you are nearly there. You *set off* or *set out* on a journey, *break your journey* (stop for a while on the way) and finally *reach your destination*.

L.e: We stayed in a village well off the beaten track. The coastline is unspoilt and breathtakingly beautiful. The first leg of the journey took us from Delhi to Kathmandu. We broke our journey in Lyon for a night. Exhausted, we reached our destination after midnight.

L.p: Real adventures involve *braving the elements* (going out in bad weather), *roughing it* (living without comforts) and sometimes *taking your life in your hands* (doing something very dangerous). Explorers *venture into the unknown*, *pitch a tent* in the wilderness and *live to tell the tale* (survive a dangerous experience).

L.e: We braved the elements and climbed to the summit in a storm. We roughed it for a week, sleeping under the stars. Crossing that road on foot, you take your life in your hands. They pitched their tent beside a frozen lake. It was terrifying, but we lived to tell the tale.

units.sub: keep in shape, reach fever pitch, score an own goal

L.p: To *keep in shape* or *stay in shape*, people *take regular exercise*, *work out* in a gym or *go for a run*. If you are not fit, you are *out of shape*; if you are getting fitter, you are *building up your stamina* (your ability to keep going). Athletes *pull a muscle*, *sustain an injury* (formal) and are sometimes *out of action* for weeks.

L.e: She swims every morning to keep in shape. I'm terribly out of shape after the winter. Cycling to work has built up my stamina. He pulled a muscle in the first ten minutes. Our best player sustained a knee injury and will be out of action for a month.

L.x: My doctor told me to *take more exercise* (not *make more exercise*).

L.p: Teams *take on* their opponents, *take the lead*, *equalise* (make the score level) and *win by a narrow margin*. A one-sided game is a *walkover*, and a match with no winner ends in a *draw* (British English). Excitement in a crowd can *reach fever pitch*. A player who accidentally puts the ball into their own net *scores an own goal* – a phrase also used for any action that harms yourself.

L.e: United take on their old rivals on Saturday. The visitors took the lead after only five minutes. The home side won by a narrow margin. The final was a walkover. As the race entered its last lap, excitement reached fever pitch. Raising ticket prices was a real own goal for the club.

L.p: Athletes *set a record*, *break a record* or *equal a record*, and the best *hold the world record*. A champion *defends a title*; a challenger *wins the title* or *clinches victory* (wins in the end). A team can *suffer a defeat* or a *crushing defeat*, and someone who loses well is *a good loser*.

L.e: She broke the national record for the 400 metres. He has held the world record since 2019. The champion will defend her title in Tokyo. A late goal clinched victory for the visitors. The team suffered a crushing defeat in the semi-final.

units.sub: toy with an idea, tentative suggestion, deciding factor

L.p: Before you commit to a plan, you may *toy with the idea* of doing something (consider it, not very seriously) or *float an idea* (suggest it to see how people react). Plans can be *at the drawing-board stage* or *in the pipeline* (being prepared). You *map out a plan*, *draw up a timetable* and *set a target*. Plans may later be *put on hold* (delayed) or *shelved* (stopped, perhaps for ever).

L.e: I'm toying with the idea of retraining as a teacher. She floated the idea of a four-day week at the meeting. Several new projects are in the pipeline. We mapped out a plan for the next five years. The building work has been put on hold. The plans for a new airport were finally shelved.

L.x: I'm *toying with the idea* (not *playing with the thought*) of moving to Wales.

L.p: A *tentative suggestion* is made carefully, without certainty. You *put forward a suggestion*, *make a proposal* or *come up with an idea*. Others may *welcome a suggestion*, *take up a suggestion* (act on it), *reject a proposal* out of hand (immediately, without considering it) or *dismiss an idea*.

L.e: Can I make a tentative suggestion? Why don't we ask the parents? The committee welcomed my suggestion. The council took up our suggestion to plant more trees. The board rejected the proposal out of hand. He dismissed the idea as too expensive.

L.p: The *deciding factor* is the thing that finally makes you choose. A decision can be *a tough call* (informal) or *a no-brainer* (very easy, informal). You *weigh up the pros and cons*, *keep your options open* (avoid deciding too soon) and finally *come down in favour of* one option. A decision made in the moment is *a snap decision*; one made after a long time is *long overdue*.

L.e: The price was the deciding factor. Choosing between the two candidates was a tough call. Taking the job was a no-brainer. Let's weigh up the pros and cons before we book. I'm keeping my options open until I hear from both universities. In the end, the panel came down in favour of the cheaper design.

units.sub: star-studded cast, glowing reviews, hold your attention

L.p: A film can have a *star-studded cast* (many famous actors) and a strong supporting cast. An actor *gives a powerful performance* or a *wooden performance* (stiff, without feeling), and might *play the lead* or take the title role. Films are often *shot on location* – in a real place rather than a studio – before they are released in cinemas.

L.e: The film boasts a star-studded cast. She gives a powerful performance as the grieving mother. Unfortunately, the hero's performance is rather wooden. He plays the lead in the new crime drama. Most of the series was shot on location in Northern Ireland.

L.x: He *played the lead* (not *made the lead*) in the school play.

L.p: A novel can be *a page-turner* (exciting to read), *a gripping read* or *heavy going* (difficult and boring). A plot can be intricate, far-fetched or full of *twists and turns*, and characters can be well-drawn or one-dimensional. A book you can't put down *holds your attention*; a book you read in short sections is one you *dip into*.

L.e: Her latest thriller is a real page-turner. I found the second half heavy going. The plot is full of twists and turns. The characters are beautifully drawn. Even at six hundred pages, the book held my attention throughout. It's a good book to dip into on the train.

L.p: When critics love something, it receives *glowing reviews* or *critical acclaim*; when they hate it, it *is panned* or *slated* (British English, informal). A film can become a *cult classic*, *break box-office records* or *flop* (fail completely). A book that sells extremely well becomes *a bestseller*.

L.e: The play received glowing reviews in all the national papers. Her debut novel won critical acclaim. The film was panned by the critics but loved by audiences. Twenty years later, it has become a cult classic. The sequel broke box-office records. His first book flopped, but his second was a bestseller.

units.sub: minimise danger, grant permission, faceless bureaucrats

L.p: Authorities *lay down rules* or guidelines, and people must *abide by the rules* (obey them) or, in formal language, *comply with regulations*. Rules aim to *minimise danger* or minimise the risk of accidents. People who *flout a rule* break it openly, without caring; when authorities become stricter, they *tighten the rules*.

L.e: The council has laid down strict rules for street parties. All visitors must abide by the safety rules. Factories must comply with regulations on noise. The new barriers should minimise the danger to cyclists. Some drivers flout the speed limit every day. The government plans to tighten the rules on gambling.

L.x: Everyone must *abide by* (not *abide to*) the rules of the club.

L.p: An authority can *grant permission* (formal), *give the go-ahead* (informal) or refuse permission. You *apply for a permit* or a licence and wait for approval. When a body *revokes a licence*, it officially takes it back. Some activities are *strictly prohibited*.

L.e: The council granted permission for the new library. The project finally got the go-ahead last month. You need to apply for a permit to fish in the lake. The club's licence was revoked after the fight. Smoking is strictly prohibited on all trains.

L.p: People often complain about *faceless bureaucrats* (officials who seem impersonal and unhelpful) and *red tape* (too many official rules and forms). You may have to *go through the proper channels* – follow the official procedure. Officials who use their power wrongly *abuse their power*, and the person who really decides things *calls the shots* (informal).

L.e: Decisions are made by faceless bureaucrats in a distant office. Starting a business involves a lot of red tape. Complaints must go through the proper channels. The inspector was accused of abusing his power. It's the owner who calls the shots here.

units.sub: dump waste, searing heat, offset carbon emissions

L.p: Factories sometimes *dump waste* illegally; in British English, dumping rubbish in the street or the countryside is *fly-tipping*. Pollution can *contaminate water supplies* and *pose a threat* to wildlife. Governments try to *cut pollution*, reduce waste and encourage recycling.

L.e: The company was fined for dumping toxic waste at sea. Fly-tipping is a growing problem in rural lanes. Chemicals from the mine contaminated the water supply. Plastic in the oceans poses a serious threat to wildlife. The city has cut air pollution by a third.

L.x: Plastic waste *poses a threat* (not *makes a threat*) to sea birds.

L.p: Climate change brings extreme weather: *searing heat* (extreme heat), *prolonged drought*, *torrential rain* and *freak storms* (very unusual ones). Temperatures soar or plunge, sea levels rise and ice caps melt. Scientists warn of *irreversible damage* – harm that can never be undone.

L.e: Southern Europe sweltered in searing heat this summer. A prolonged drought has destroyed this year's harvest. Torrential rain caused flash floods across the region. A freak storm hit the island in October. Rising sea levels threaten coastal towns. Scientists fear the damage may be irreversible.

L.p: People try to *reduce their carbon footprint* – the amount of carbon dioxide their lifestyle produces. Companies *offset carbon emissions* by paying for projects that remove carbon elsewhere, such as planting forests. Governments set targets, switch to *renewable energy* and protect *endangered species*, while campaigners *lobby the government* (try to influence it).

L.e: We've reduced our carbon footprint by taking fewer flights. Some airlines let passengers offset their carbon emissions. The country aims to switch to renewable energy by 2040. The reserve protects several endangered species. Environmental groups are lobbying the government for stricter laws.

units.sub: back of beyond, rural idyll, urban regeneration

L.p: Many city dwellers dream of a *rural idyll* – a peaceful, perfect life in the countryside. In reality, a village may be in *the back of beyond* (informal) or *in the middle of nowhere*, far from any town. Country life can mean a *slower pace of life* and a *close-knit community*, but also poor transport links and *few amenities* (shops, services and facilities).

L.e: They sold their flat and went in search of a rural idyll. My grandparents live in the back of beyond. We got lost in the middle of nowhere. I love the slower pace of life here. It's a close-knit community where everybody knows everybody. The village has few amenities – not even a shop.

L.x: They live in *the middle of nowhere* (not *the centre of nowhere*).

L.p: Cities offer a *vibrant nightlife* and a cosmopolitan atmosphere, but also *traffic congestion*, noise and a *high cost of living*. Some areas are *run-down* (in poor condition), while others are *up-and-coming* (becoming popular). *Urban sprawl* is the uncontrolled spread of a city into the countryside around it.

L.e: The city has a vibrant nightlife and a cosmopolitan atmosphere. Traffic congestion is worst on Friday afternoons. The capital has a very high cost of living. Our street used to be run-down, but now it's up-and-coming. Urban sprawl has swallowed up several villages.

L.p: Councils try to improve run-down districts through *urban regeneration*, and a successful project can *breathe new life into* an old area. *Derelict buildings* (empty and falling apart) are converted into flats and studios. Critics say that gentrification – wealthier people moving in – can push up prices and drive out the original residents.

L.e: The urban regeneration scheme transformed the docks. The new market has breathed new life into the old town centre. Derelict warehouses are being converted into luxury flats. Gentrification has pushed up rents in the area.

units.sub: clear your debts, agreed credit limit, identity theft

L.p: To *manage your finances* well, you *draw up a budget*, *live within your means* (spend no more than you earn) and *put money aside* for the future. Some people live beyond their means and *run up debts*. Regular bills *eat into* your income, leaving less to spend.

L.e: Since I lost my job, I've had to draw up a strict budget. We try to live within our means. I put a little money aside every month. He ran up huge debts on his credit cards. Rent eats into most of my salary.

L.x: We try to *live within our means* (not *live inside our means*).

L.p: You *take out a mortgage* (a loan to buy a home) and repay it in *monthly instalments*. A credit card comes with an *agreed credit limit* – the most you may borrow – and you can exceed it or, informally, max out the card. When you *clear your debts*, you no longer owe anything; people in serious trouble *fall behind with payments*.

L.e: We took out a mortgage on a small flat. I'm paying for the car in monthly instalments. The shop refused my card because I'd gone over my agreed credit limit. It took me five years to clear my debts. They fell behind with their mortgage payments and lost the house.

L.p: You open an account, pay money in, *withdraw cash* and *transfer money* online. Your account may be in credit or *overdrawn* – with more taken out than was in it. Criminals commit *identity theft* by stealing personal details, so banks advise customers never to share their PIN and to *report suspicious activity* at once.

L.e: You can withdraw cash at any branch. I transferred the money to my sister last night. My account is overdrawn again. Identity theft is one of the fastest-growing crimes. Report any suspicious activity on your account immediately.

units.sub: curb inflation, safeguard your interests, plummeting profits

L.p: Central banks try to *curb inflation* or *keep inflation in check*. When prices rise fast, *inflation soars* or spirals out of control; when it falls, it eases. Banks *raise interest rates* or cut them, and governments either increase public spending or *slash spending* (cut it hard). Economists forecast growth and often have to revise their forecasts.

L.e: The bank raised interest rates to curb inflation. Inflation soared to fifteen per cent in the 1970s. Price rises eased slightly last month. The government has slashed spending on roads. Economists have revised their growth forecasts downwards.

L.x: The bank acted to *curb inflation* (not *brake inflation*).

L.p: In a boom, the economy grows rapidly and unemployment falls. In a recession, the economy shrinks and many businesses *go bankrupt*. *Plummeting profits* and falling *share prices* hit investors, and *consumer confidence* – people's willingness to spend – is low. Later, the economy may *bounce back* or recover more slowly.

L.e: The housing market boomed in the early 2000s. Hundreds of small firms went bankrupt during the recession. Plummeting profits forced the company to close two factories. Share prices plunged after the announcement. Consumer confidence is at its lowest level for years. The economy bounced back faster than expected.

L.p: Businesses and governments *safeguard their interests* (protect them) and try to protect jobs. Countries *impose tariffs* on imports or lift restrictions on trade. Companies *cut costs*, streamline their operations and sometimes *shed jobs* (reduce staff). In a crisis, a government may *bail out* a bank – give it money to prevent its collapse.

L.e: The new law will safeguard the interests of small farmers. The government imposed tariffs on imported steel. The firm is cutting costs by closing its city offices. The airline plans to shed two thousand jobs. Taxpayers' money was used to bail out the banks.

units.sub: antisocial behaviour, dysfunctional family, unfit for human habitation

L.p: Social problems include *antisocial behaviour* (behaviour that harms or annoys others, such as vandalism), *petty crime* (minor crime), drug abuse and homelessness. People *sleep rough* (British English) when they have nowhere to live. Some children grow up in a *dysfunctional family*, where relationships are badly damaged, or in *abject poverty* (extreme poverty).

L.e: Residents complain of antisocial behaviour in the park at night. Petty crime has risen in the town centre. More people are sleeping rough than ten years ago. He grew up in a dysfunctional family and left home at fifteen. Millions still live in abject poverty.

L.x: Hundreds of people are *sleeping rough* (not *sleeping hard*) in the city.

L.p: Some housing is so poor or dangerous that it is *unfit for human habitation*. Families may live in *overcrowded conditions*, and cities need more *affordable housing* – homes that people on low incomes can pay for. Many households struggle to *make ends meet* (have just enough money to live on).

L.e: Inspectors declared the flats unfit for human habitation. Six of us lived in overcrowded conditions in a two-bedroom flat. The city needs to provide more affordable housing. Many pensioners struggle to make ends meet.

L.p: Governments and charities *tackle the problem*, address the issue and *combat crime*. They *launch an initiative* and *allocate funds* (give money for a particular purpose). Some vulnerable people *fall through the net* – they are missed by the system that should help them. The long-term aim is to *break the cycle* of poverty.

L.e: The council has launched an initiative to tackle loneliness among older people. New funds have been allocated to combat youth crime. Too many vulnerable children fall through the net. Education is the best way to break the cycle of poverty.

units.sub: harness technology, cutting-edge design, wireless hotspot

L.p: Scientists *conduct research* and *test a theory* through experiments. A team may *make a breakthrough*, *publish their findings* and have their work checked by other experts. *Groundbreaking* research is completely new and important, and it can *push back the boundaries* of knowledge. Results must be repeated by others before they are widely accepted.

L.e: The team has made a breakthrough in battery technology. They published their findings in a leading journal. Her groundbreaking work changed our understanding of sleep. Space research pushes back the boundaries of what we know. Other labs have so far failed to repeat the results.

L.x: The scientists *made a breakthrough* (not *did a breakthrough*) in cancer treatment.

L.p: Engineers *harness technology* – control and use it – to solve problems. The newest designs are *cutting-edge* or *state-of-the-art*. Technology can *become obsolete* (no longer used) or *revolutionise* an industry, and people who try new gadgets before everyone else are early adopters.

L.e: Farmers are harnessing technology to save water. The car has a cutting-edge design. The hospital has state-of-the-art equipment. Fax machines became obsolete almost overnight. Smartphones revolutionised the way we take photos.

L.p: Today we go online through *wireless hotspots* (places with public internet access), *stream films* and music and *store data* in the cloud. Software needs regular updates, and systems can crash or be hacked. Many new technologies *raise ethical questions* about privacy and fairness.

L.e: The café has a free wireless hotspot. I stream most of my music now. All our photos are stored in the cloud. The hospital's computer system was hacked last week. Artificial intelligence raises serious ethical questions.

units.sub: build up resistance, adverse reaction, shake off a cold

L.p: You catch a cold or *come down with* flu (start to have it), and a nasty cough can be hard to *shake off* (get rid of). An illness can be mild, serious, terminal or *chronic* (long-lasting). When you *run a temperature*, you have a fever. A *disease spreads* when more and more people catch it.

L.e: I've come down with a cold and can't shake it off. My son was running a temperature all night. Asthma is a chronic condition that can be controlled. The disease spread rapidly through the camp. A nasty bug is going round the office.

L.x: I think I've *come down with* (not *come up with*) flu.

L.p: A doctor *makes a diagnosis*, *prescribes medication* and may refer you to a specialist. Patients *undergo surgery* (formal) or have an operation. Some drugs cause side effects, and a patient can have an *adverse reaction* – a harmful effect – to a medicine. A patient who is getting better is *on the mend*; one who becomes ill again *suffers a relapse*.

L.e: It took the doctors a month to make a diagnosis. He underwent surgery on his knee last week. Some patients suffered an adverse reaction to the vaccine. Grandma is on the mend after her fall. He was making good progress until he suffered a relapse.

L.p: The body *builds up resistance* to infections, and vaccines help to *boost the immune system*. Doctors advise people to eat a balanced diet and cut down on salt and sugar. Bad habits *take their toll on* your health – they damage it slowly. Someone who looks very well is *the picture of health*.

L.e: Children build up resistance to common illnesses at nursery. Getting enough sleep helps to boost your immune system. Years of night shifts took their toll on his health. At ninety, Grandad is the picture of health.

units.sub: custodial sentence, beyond reasonable doubt, trumped-up charges

L.p: Criminals *commit an offence* or break the law. The police *launch an investigation*, *gather evidence* and make arrests, *taking* suspects *into custody*. A suspect may be charged or *released without charge*. Someone arrested on *trumped-up charges* has been falsely accused, often for political reasons.

L.e: He committed his first offence at the age of fourteen. Detectives have launched an investigation into the fire. Police made two arrests after the match. The suspect was taken into custody overnight. She was released without charge. The journalist was jailed on trumped-up charges.

L.x: The gang *committed* (not *made*) a series of robberies.

L.p: A case *goes to trial*, and the defendant *pleads guilty* or not guilty. Witnesses *give evidence*. The jury must be sure of guilt *beyond reasonable doubt* before they *reach a verdict*. A defendant may be found guilty or acquitted (found not guilty). An unfair verdict is *a miscarriage of justice*.

L.e: The case is expected to go to trial next spring. He pleaded not guilty to all the charges. Three witnesses gave evidence for the defence. The jury must be convinced beyond reasonable doubt. After two days, the jury reached a unanimous verdict. The men spent ten years in prison before the miscarriage of justice was recognised.

L.p: A judge passes sentence. A *custodial sentence* means time in prison; a non-custodial one might be a fine or community service. Prisoners *serve a sentence* and may be released on parole. A *suspended sentence* only begins if the offender breaks the law again. Some people complain that sentences are too lenient; others find them harsh.

L.e: First-time offenders rarely receive a custodial sentence. She was ordered to do 200 hours of community service. He served six years of a ten-year sentence. The driver got a suspended sentence. Victims' groups say the punishment was far too lenient.

units.sub: deploy troops, pre-emptive strike, collateral damage

L.p: When *tensions escalate*, countries may go to war. Governments *deploy troops* (send them into position) and *launch an offensive*. A *pre-emptive strike* is an attack made to stop the enemy attacking first. Soldiers *come under fire*, and armies can *suffer heavy losses*.

L.e: Tensions escalated after the border incident. The government has deployed troops along the frontier. The army launched a major offensive in the spring. Some argued for a pre-emptive strike against the missile sites. The soldiers came under fire as they crossed the river. Both sides suffered heavy losses.

L.x: The general decided to *launch an attack* (not *throw an attack*) at dawn.

L.p: War causes *civilian casualties* – deaths and injuries among people who are not soldiers. *Collateral damage* is a military term for unintended harm to civilians or buildings. Many people *flee the fighting* and become refugees. Cities can be *reduced to rubble*, leaving whole regions *war-torn*.

L.e: The bombing caused heavy civilian casualties. Officials described the destroyed hospital as collateral damage. Thousands fled the fighting with only what they could carry. Much of the old city was reduced to rubble. Aid is finally reaching the war-torn region.

L.p: To end a conflict, the two sides *call a ceasefire*, *hold peace talks* and *negotiate a settlement*. They sign a peace treaty, and international forces may be sent to keep the peace. A *fragile peace* could easily break down; the hope is always for a lasting one.

L.e: The two sides called a ceasefire on Christmas Eve. Peace talks are due to resume next week. They finally negotiated a settlement after five years of war. UN forces are monitoring the border. The peace remains fragile.
