units.sub: lifelong friends, platonic relationship, heal the rift

L.p: *Lifelong friends* have known each other for most of their lives. A *casual acquaintance* is someone you know only slightly, and a *fair-weather friend* is only around when things are going well. A *platonic relationship* is a close friendship with no romance in it. People *strike up a friendship* when they start one, and *forge a friendship* when they build a strong one.

L.e: Tom and I have been lifelong friends since primary school. She's more of a casual acquaintance than a friend. When I lost my job, I found out who were just fair-weather friends. Theirs is a purely platonic relationship. The two leaders forged a friendship during the talks.

L.x: We *struck up a friendship* (not *hit a friendship*) on the train to Glasgow.

L.p: Good friends *stand by* each other in difficult times, even if they don't always *see eye to eye* (agree). Old friends *go back a long way*. You *confide in* a close friend when you tell them your secrets, and a true friend will *go out of their way* – make a special effort – to help you.

L.e: My friends stood by me when I was ill. We don't always see eye to eye, but we never stay angry for long. Ben and I go back a long way. I can confide in my sister about anything. He went out of his way to help me move house.

L.p: Friends can *fall out* (argue and stop being friendly) or *drift apart* (slowly become less close). A serious disagreement creates a rift between people. To end it, they make up, *bury the hatchet* (agree to stop arguing) or *heal the rift*. Sometimes it takes years to rebuild trust.

L.e: The brothers fell out over their father's will. We drifted apart after university. The argument caused a rift between the two families. After ten years of silence, they finally buried the hatchet. A long phone call helped to heal the rift.

units.sub: child prodigy, midlife crisis, senior moment

L.p: A *child prodigy* shows exceptional talent at a very young age. Young people *come of age* (become adults, legally or symbolically) and eventually *leave the nest* (leave their parents' home). A teenager who behaves strangely for a while may just be *going through a phase*. Your *formative years* are the years when your character develops.

L.e: Mozart was a child prodigy who composed music at five. In many countries, turning eighteen means coming of age. Our youngest has just left the nest. Don't worry about his hair – he's just going through a phase. She spent her formative years in Hong Kong.

L.x: She *came of age* (not *became of age*) during the war.

L.p: People in their forties and fifties may feel *in the prime of life*. Some go through a *midlife crisis* – a period of doubt that can lead to sudden changes. People *put down roots* (settle in a place) and *reach milestones* such as a fiftieth birthday. When you begin to feel older, *age is catching up with* you.

L.e: At fifty, she felt she was in the prime of life. He went through a midlife crisis and bought a motorbike. After years of travelling, they put down roots in Devon. Turning forty is a major milestone. I can't run as fast as I used to – age is catching up with me.

L.p: Older people may be *getting on* (informal) or, formally, advancing in years. They *draw a pension* and enjoy their retirement. Someone who still feels and acts young is *young at heart*. A moment of forgetfulness is jokingly called *a senior moment*, and people who *live to a ripe old age* live a very long life.

L.e: My grandfather is getting on, but he still walks every day. She has drawn a pension for twenty years. At ninety-two, she's still young at heart. I've just put the milk in the oven – I'm having a senior moment! Both my great-grandmothers lived to a ripe old age.

units.sub: go into rehab, kiss and tell, heap praise on

L.p: Some people rise slowly to fame; others *shoot to fame* overnight. A celebrity is *in the public eye* and may *court publicity* (try to attract it). Fame can be *fleeting* – here today, gone tomorrow – and some stars *fade into obscurity* (are gradually forgotten).

L.e: She shot to fame after winning a TV talent show. He has been in the public eye for thirty years. Some celebrities court publicity wherever they go. Their fame was fleeting. After one hit record, the band faded into obscurity.

L.x: She *shot to fame* (not *jumped to fame*) after her first film.

L.p: Tabloid newspapers dig up dirt on celebrities and *invade their privacy*. A *kiss-and-tell* story is sold to a newspaper by a former partner. Stars with addictions may *go into rehab* (a clinic for treating addiction). A scandal can *tarnish someone's image*, but a fallen star sometimes *makes a comeback*.

L.e: Photographers camped outside her house, invading her privacy. His ex-girlfriend sold a kiss-and-tell story to a Sunday paper. The singer went into rehab for the second time. The scandal tarnished the team's image. After ten years away, she made a spectacular comeback.

L.p: A real hero *risks their life* or shows great courage. Newspapers *heap praise on* heroes (praise them a great deal), and some become a *household name* – known by everyone. Others remain *unsung heroes*, doing great work without recognition. Heroes often become *role models* for young people.

L.e: The firefighter risked his life to save the children. The newspapers heaped praise on the young volunteers. After the rescue, the pilot became a household name. Carers are the unsung heroes of our society. Athletes should remember that they are role models.

units.sub: bone idle, poison the atmosphere, nasty piece of work

L.p: Informal British English has strong ways of criticising people. Someone extremely lazy is *bone idle*, and someone who doesn't do their share *doesn't pull their weight*. An incompetent person *makes a hash of* things (does them badly) or is simply *not up to the job*. Someone who can never find anything or arrive on time is *hopelessly disorganised*.

L.e: Her son is bone idle – he won't even make his own bed. Some members of the team aren't pulling their weight. I made a complete hash of the interview. Frankly, the new manager isn't up to the job. My brother is hopelessly disorganised.

L.x: He's *hopelessly disorganised* (not *hopefully disorganised*) – he loses everything.

L.p: A *nasty piece of work* is an unpleasant, unkind person (informal). Someone who creates bad feeling *poisons the atmosphere*, *stirs up trouble* or spreads *malicious rumours* (untrue stories meant to harm). Rudeness can be mild or *downright rude* – completely rude.

L.e: Her ex-husband is a nasty piece of work. His constant complaints poisoned the atmosphere in the office. She's always stirring up trouble between colleagues. Someone has been spreading malicious rumours about me. The waiter was downright rude to us.

L.p: When you criticise someone directly, you *tell them a few home truths* (unpleasant facts about themselves), *give them a piece of your mind* (tell them angrily what you think) or *take them to task* (criticise them strongly). Less directly, you *have a dig at* someone or *damn them with faint praise* – praise them so weakly that it sounds like criticism.

L.e: It was time someone told him a few home truths. I gave the builder a piece of my mind. The minister was taken to task for his comments. She keeps having a dig at me about my cooking. The reviewer damned the novel with faint praise, calling it 'perfectly readable'.

units.sub: act as a referee, accumulate experience, financial acumen

L.p: When someone applies for a job, they ask a former employer or teacher to *act as a referee* or *provide a reference*. A *glowing reference* is very positive; a lukewarm one is not enthusiastic. A referee may *vouch for* someone (say they are honest and reliable) and recommend them *without reservation* – with no doubts at all.

L.e: My old professor has agreed to act as a referee. Could you provide a reference for my visa application? Her manager wrote her a glowing reference. A lukewarm reference can cost you the job. I can vouch for his honesty. I recommend her without reservation.

L.p: References describe how someone has *accumulated experience* in a field and *acquired skills*. A candidate may have *financial acumen* (skill with money and business), a *proven track record* (a history of success) and excellent interpersonal skills. Employers want people who *work well under pressure* and meet deadlines.

L.e: Over ten years she has accumulated wide experience in hospital management. He acquired valuable skills during his time abroad. Her financial acumen makes her ideal for the role. He has a proven track record in sales. She works well under pressure and always meets deadlines.

L.x: She has *gained experience* (not *won experience*) in several countries.

L.p: Referees describe character with phrases such as *a conscientious worker* (careful and hard-working), *a valuable member of the team* and a natural leader. A young candidate may *show great promise* and *rise to a challenge* (deal well with something difficult). Some references end by saying that the person *will be sorely missed*.

L.e: Daniel is a conscientious worker who never cuts corners. She has been a valuable member of the team for six years. This young designer shows great promise. She always rises to a challenge. Her cheerful presence will be sorely missed.

L.p: Descriptions of appearance use fixed partnerships: *a slender figure*, *a weather-beaten face* (lined from years outdoors), *piercing* blue *eyes* and *a receding hairline* (hair that is disappearing from the forehead). Someone may *bear a striking resemblance* to a relative, or be *the spitting image* of a parent (informal) – look exactly like them.

L.e: The old fisherman had a weather-beaten face and piercing blue eyes. My dad has a receding hairline but refuses to admit it. In old photos, my nephew bears a striking resemblance to our great-uncle Fred. He's the spitting image of his father at that age.

L.x: She *bears a striking resemblance* (not *carries a striking resemblance*) to her aunt.

L.p: Personality collocations often combine a quality with an intensifier: someone has *boundless energy* (energy that seems to have no limit), *a stubborn streak* (a tendency to be stubborn at times) or *a wicked sense of humour* (clever and slightly unkind). People can be *painfully shy* or *fiercely independent*.

L.e: Our new puppy has boundless energy. She's lovely, but she has a stubborn streak. My uncle has a wicked sense of humour. He was painfully shy as a teenager. Grandma is fiercely independent and won't accept help.

L.p: You tell someone to *act their age* when they are behaving childishly. A person who suddenly becomes very angry *flies off the handle* (informal). A shy person can gradually *come out of their shell*, while someone who shows their feelings openly *wears their heart on their sleeve*.

L.e: Stop throwing food and act your age! He flies off the handle at the smallest thing. At university she really came out of her shell. He wears his heart on his sleeve – you always know how he feels.

units.sub: cramped conditions, waste of space, go down in history

L.p: Time can drag (pass slowly) or fly. You *while away the time* when you spend it pleasantly while waiting, and you *make up for lost time* when you do a lot of something you missed earlier. Good things *stand the test of time* (stay good for many years), great events *go down in history*, and a change that should have happened much earlier is *long overdue*.

L.e: The afternoon dragged as we waited for news. We whiled away the hours playing cards. After his illness, he's making up for lost time. Her novels have stood the test of time. That match will go down in history. The reforms are long overdue.

L.p: People sometimes live or work in *cramped conditions* or a *confined space*, and a city can be *densely populated*. Something useless that just sits there is *a waste of space* (informal, and unkind when said about a person). You *make room for* new things, and big objects *take up* a lot of space.

L.e: The refugees were living in cramped conditions. Engineers had to work in a confined space under the floor. Hong Kong is one of the most densely populated places on earth. That old wardrobe is a waste of space. We need to make room for the new sofa.

L.x: We moved the desk to *make room for* (not *do room for*) a bookcase.

L.p: Places can be *within walking distance* or just *a stone's throw from* somewhere (very close). You *keep your distance* when you stay away from something, and *keep someone at arm's length* when you avoid becoming close to them. Something *in the vicinity* is nearby (formal).

L.e: The hotel is within walking distance of the beach. We live a stone's throw from the station. The deer kept its distance from us. She tends to keep new colleagues at arm's length. Police are looking for anyone seen in the vicinity of the bank.

units.sub: husky voice, incessant noise, let out a cry

L.p: A voice can be *husky* (low and rough, often attractive), *hoarse* (rough because of illness or shouting), *shrill* (high and unpleasant), soothing or booming. You *raise your voice* when you speak louder, often in anger, and you can *lose your voice* when you have a cold. Before a speech, people often *clear their throat*.

L.e: The singer has a husky voice that suits the blues. After the match I was hoarse from shouting. The teacher never raises her voice. I lost my voice for three days with a cold. He cleared his throat and began his speech.

L.x: I *lost my voice* (not *missed my voice*) after the concert.

L.p: Noise can be *incessant* (never stopping), *deafening* (extremely loud), *muffled* (unclear because something is in the way) or faint. People *kick up a racket* (informal) when they make a lot of noise. Sounds fade away or *die down*, and a silence can be *eerie* (strange and frightening).

L.e: The incessant noise of the traffic kept me awake. The music in the club was deafening. We heard muffled voices through the wall. The neighbours were kicking up a racket until two in the morning. Gradually the applause died down. There was an eerie silence in the abandoned village.

L.p: People *let out a cry*, a scream or a sigh. They burst out laughing or *roar with laughter*, *gasp in amazement* and groan in pain. Animals have their own verbs: dogs bark, lions roar and cats purr. A crowd can cheer, boo or fall silent.

L.e: She let out a cry when she saw the spider. The audience roared with laughter. The children gasped in amazement at the magician. The cat purred contentedly on my lap. The crowd booed the referee off the pitch.

units.sub: viable option, simplicity itself, take the easy way out

L.p: Something very easy is *simplicity itself*, *child's play*, *a piece of cake* (informal) or *plain sailing* (easy, without problems). A process can be *hassle-free* – without annoying difficulties – and you *make light work of* a job when you do it easily and quickly.

L.e: Once you know the trick, changing a tyre is simplicity itself. For an experienced chef, this recipe is child's play. The first exam was a piece of cake. After the first week, it was plain sailing. Booking online is quick and hassle-free. The new machine makes light work of the washing-up.

L.p: To make things easier, organisations *simplify a procedure* or *streamline a process* (make it simpler and more efficient). A *user-friendly* design is easy to use. You *break down a task* into stages, and good instructions are *easy to follow*.

L.e: The bank has simplified its application procedure. We streamlined the ordering process and saved hours each week. The new software is very user-friendly. Break the project down into smaller tasks. The guide is clear and easy to follow.

L.p: A *viable option* is a realistic choice that can work. You *explore the options* before you decide. If you choose the easiest course instead of the right one, you *take the easy way out*, and you *cut corners* when you do something badly to save time or money.

L.e: Selling the house may be the only viable option. Let's explore all the options before we decide. Quitting now would be taking the easy way out. The builders cut corners, and now the roof leaks.

L.x: The builders *cut corners* (not *cut edges*) to finish early.

units.sub: severe blow, hinder progress, encounter difficulties

L.p: People and organisations *encounter difficulties* (formal) or face an *uphill struggle* – a long, hard effort. A setback can be *a severe blow* or *a bitter blow* (very disappointing). Problems can *hinder progress* (slow it down), and a situation with no chance of success is *a lost cause*.

L.e: The expedition encountered difficulties on the second day. Getting the law changed will be an uphill struggle. The closure of the factory was a severe blow to the town. Losing their captain was a bitter blow. Bad weather hindered progress on the new bridge. Some people say the campaign is a lost cause.

L.x: The news was *a bitter blow* (not *a sour blow*) to the fans.

L.p: A *thorny issue* is complicated and hard to deal with, and a plan *fraught with difficulty* is full of problems. You can be *in a tight spot* (informal), *in deep water* (in serious trouble) or between a rock and a hard place. A request that is very hard to meet is *a tall order*.

L.e: Immigration is a thorny issue for any government. Negotiating with both sides is fraught with difficulty. I'm in a bit of a tight spot – could you lend me twenty pounds? If the boss finds out, you'll be in deep water. Finishing the whole report by Friday is a tall order.

L.p: You *overcome an obstacle*, or you *get round a problem* by finding a way to avoid it. A patient who survives a dangerous illness *pulls through*. Before a plan can work, people often need to *iron out problems* – solve the small difficulties that remain.

L.e: She overcame many obstacles to become a doctor. We got round the problem by borrowing a van. Doctors say he is expected to pull through. We need a meeting to iron out a few problems.

units.sub: finite number, endless supply, unknown quantity

L.p: Quantities can be vast, *substantial* (large and important), *negligible* (too small to matter) or minute (extremely small). You can speak of a *finite number* (a limited number) or an *endless supply* – an amount that never seems to run out. A small part of something is *a fraction of* it, and the largest part is *the lion's share*.

L.e: The project will cost a substantial amount of money. The risk to the public is negligible. There is only a finite number of tickets left. The children seem to have an endless supply of energy. The repairs cost a fraction of the price of a new car. The eldest son inherited the lion's share of the estate.

L.x: The difference in price is *negligible* (not *negligent*).

L.p: Things can be *of modest proportions* (not large) or of epic proportions. A problem can *reach epidemic proportions* (become very widespread) or grow *out of all proportion* – far bigger than it should be. People sometimes *underestimate the scale* of a problem, and a plan can be *scaled down* (made smaller).

L.e: The house was of modest proportions but beautifully designed. Obesity has reached epidemic proportions in some countries. A small disagreement grew out of all proportion. We underestimated the scale of the damage. The council has scaled down its plans for the new stadium.

L.p: An *unknown quantity* is a person or thing whose abilities or effects are not yet known. A *ballpark figure* (informal) is a rough estimate. Costs can *run into millions*, and something that is scarce is *in short supply*.

L.e: The new goalkeeper is still an unknown quantity. Can you give me a ballpark figure for the repairs? The cost of the damage runs into millions. Fresh water is in short supply.

units.sub: sweeping changes, make a change, sudden shift

L.p: Changes can be *sweeping* (affecting many things), *radical* (deep and complete) or *far-reaching* (with wide effects). Governments *implement changes* (put them into practice), and campaigns *bring about change*. A moment after which things are never the same again is *a turning point*.

L.e: The new director made sweeping changes to the company. The report calls for radical change in the way schools are funded. The reforms will have far-reaching consequences. It took two years to implement the changes. Moving to Japan was a turning point in my life.

L.x: The government *implemented* (not *realised*) the changes very quickly.

L.p: There can be *a sudden shift* in opinion or *a change of heart* (a change of opinion or feeling). Politicians sometimes *do a U-turn* – completely change a plan or policy. When a situation is completely reversed, *the tables are turned*.

L.e: Polls this week show a sudden shift away from the ruling party. She had a change of heart and decided to stay. The minister did a U-turn on tuition fees. Now the tables are turned – it's our team that's winning.

L.p: You *make a change* when you start doing something differently. A situation can *take a turn for the worse* (or the better). Something different and pleasant *makes a nice change*. People *turn over a new leaf* when they start behaving better, and a place can *change beyond recognition*.

L.e: I've decided to make a change and work part-time. Her health has taken a turn for the worse. A quiet weekend would make a nice change. After his arrest, he promised to turn over a new leaf. The town centre has changed beyond recognition.

units.sub: bring to a halt, close off a street, dispel rumours

L.p: An accident can *bring traffic to a halt*, and production can *grind to a halt* (slowly stop completely). People *put a stop to* bad behaviour and *call off* events. A company that closes *ceases trading* (formal), and a project or programme can be *axed* (informal).

L.e: A broken-down lorry brought traffic to a halt. Production ground to a halt during the strike. Parents want to put a stop to bullying. The match was called off because of snow. The shop ceased trading last year. The TV series was axed after two seasons.

L.x: Production *ground to a halt* (not *grinded to a halt*) during the strike.

L.p: Police *close off a street* or *cordon off* an area (put a barrier round it), and train companies *suspend services* in bad weather. To stop false stories, people *dispel rumours* or *put the record straight* – correct the false information.

L.e: Police closed off the street after the explosion. The area was cordoned off while experts examined the package. Train services have been suspended because of flooding. The club issued a statement to dispel rumours about the manager. The minister put the record straight in a TV interview.

L.p: You launch a project or *embark on a career* (formal). Events *get under way* (start), and a team can *get off to a flying start* (begin very successfully) – or you can get off on the wrong foot with someone. To start an activity or discussion, you *set the ball rolling*.

L.e: She embarked on a career in law at forty. The festival gets under way on Friday. The team got off to a flying start with three wins. I'm afraid we got off on the wrong foot. Let me set the ball rolling with a few questions.

units.sub: root cause, provoke an outcry, dire consequences

L.p: The *root cause* of a problem is its basic, original cause; an *underlying cause* is hidden beneath the surface. Something can be *a contributing factor* – one of several causes. Events *give rise to* problems (formal), *provoke an outcry* (cause public anger) or *set off a chain reaction*, in which one event leads to the next.

L.e: Poverty is the root cause of much crime. Stress may be an underlying cause of the illness. Bad weather was a contributing factor in the crash. The decision gave rise to widespread concern. The new tax provoked an outcry. One cancelled flight set off a chain reaction of delays.

L.x: The new law *provoked an outcry* (not *made an outcry*) among farmers.

L.p: Actions have consequences, and consequences can be *dire* (very serious), unforeseen or *unintended*. Something can *have a profound effect on* people's lives. In British English, an indirect effect on other things is a *knock-on effect*.

L.e: If we ignore the warnings, the consequences will be dire. The policy had several unintended consequences. Her teacher had a profound effect on her life. The strike had a knock-on effect on other industries.

L.p: In formal writing, you can say that something is *attributable to* a cause, *stems from* it or *can be traced back to* it. One thing *results in* another. Researchers *draw a link between* two things when they show that they are connected.

L.e: The accident was attributable to human error. Many of his problems stem from his childhood. The tradition can be traced back to the Middle Ages. The new road resulted in less traffic in the village. Researchers have drawn a link between diet and memory.

units.sub: swarm of bees, flurry of activity, stroke of genius

L.h: A Groups of animals and people

L.p: English has special words for groups. Insects come in a *swarm*, birds in a *flock*, cattle in a *herd* and fish in a *shoal*. Many of these words are also used metaphorically: *a swarm of tourists*, *a flock of admirers*. A story that is completely untrue is *a pack of lies*.

L.e: A swarm of bees settled on the garden wall. A flock of geese flew overhead. A herd of cattle blocked the lane. A shoal of tiny fish darted past the boat. Swarms of tourists filled the square. Everything he told the police was a pack of lies.

L.x: We saw *a flock of* (not *a herd of*) sheep on the hillside.

L.p: Some nouns describe a short burst: *a flurry of activity* (a lot of sudden activity), *a burst of applause*, *a spate of* burglaries (a lot of them in a short time). Others describe tiny amounts: *a shred of evidence*, *a grain of truth* and *a glimmer of hope* (a small sign of hope).

L.e: The kitchen burst into a flurry of activity when the bride's car pulled up. The speech was met with a burst of applause. Police are investigating a spate of burglaries in the area. There isn't a shred of evidence against him. There's a grain of truth in what she says. After weeks of talks, there is a glimmer of hope.

L.p: *A stroke of genius* is a brilliant idea, and *a stroke of luck* is a lucky event. Uncountable nouns need a partner word: *a piece of advice*, *a word of warning*, *an item of clothing*. These partnerships are fixed – you can't say *an advice* or *a luck*.

L.e: Hiring a local guide was a stroke of genius. By a stroke of luck, the bus was late too. Can I give you a piece of advice? A word of warning: the roads are icy. Each passenger may bring one item of hand luggage.

units.sub: bear little resemblance to, polar opposites, draw a comparison

L.p: Two things can *bear a close resemblance to* each other; if they are not alike, one *bears little resemblance to* the other. You *draw a comparison between* things, and *draw a parallel between* them when you show how they are similar. People with different views can still *find common ground*. In informal British English, things that are much the same are *much of a muchness*.

L.e: The film bears little resemblance to the book. The new office bears a close resemblance to a glass box. Historians have drawn parallels between the two empires. Despite our differences, we found common ground on education. The three hotels are much of a muchness.

L.x: Writers often *draw a parallel* (not *make a parallel*) between the two empires.

L.p: Two people can be *polar opposites* (completely different) or *worlds apart*. There can be a *stark contrast* (a very clear one) or a *subtle difference* between things. The law and dictionaries *make a distinction between* similar ideas.

L.e: My brother and I are polar opposites. Their views on education are worlds apart. There is a stark contrast between the old town and the new suburbs. There's only a subtle difference between the two shades. The law makes a distinction between theft and robbery.

L.p: In formal writing, one thing *compares favourably with* another (is better than it) or *pales in comparison with* it (seems less important or impressive). Something can *stand in contrast to* something else. If nothing is better, it is *second to none*.

L.e: Our results compare favourably with those of other schools. Last year's problems pale in comparison with this year's. Her calm style stands in sharp contrast to her predecessor's. The service at this hotel is second to none.

units.sub: give it your best shot, abortive attempt, worth a try

L.p: If you try as hard as you can, you *give it your best shot* (informal), *do your utmost* (formal) or *go all out*. You *make every effort* (formal) to achieve something, and you *bend over backwards* when you try very hard to help or please someone. Something that might succeed is *worth a try*.

L.e: Whatever happens, just give it your best shot. We will do our utmost to find your luggage. The team went all out to win the cup. The hotel staff bent over backwards to help us. It's a long shot, but it's worth a try.

L.x: We will *make every effort* (not *do every effort*) to help you.

L.p: An attempt can be determined, desperate, *half-hearted* (without much effort) or *abortive* (failed, formal). Hard work can *pay off* (bring success) or *bear fruit*, but you sometimes *try in vain* – without any success at all.

L.e: He made a half-hearted attempt to tidy his room. After two abortive attempts, the rocket was finally launched. All her hard work paid off when she got the scholarship. Years of research have finally borne fruit. I tried in vain to persuade her.

L.p: A *concerted effort* is made by many people together. Organisers *spare no effort* (do everything possible), and people *go to great lengths* to get what they want. If you work late into the night, you *burn the midnight oil*.

L.e: A concerted effort by local residents saved the library. The organisers spared no effort to make the festival a success. She went to great lengths to find her birth mother. I burned the midnight oil before the exam.

units.sub: not lose any sleep, to be brutally honest, on the go

L.p: Conversation is full of fixed collocations. You *won't lose any sleep over* something that doesn't worry you. If you are very busy, you are *on the go* or *rushed off your feet*. You *keep someone posted* (give them the latest news) and *catch up with* friends you haven't seen for a while.

L.e: If they don't invite me, I won't lose any sleep over it. I've been on the go since six this morning. We were rushed off our feet in the shop on Saturday. Keep me posted about the interview. I'm catching up with an old school friend tonight.

L.x: We were *rushed off our feet* (not *rushed off our legs*) all day.

L.p: Speakers soften or strengthen opinions with fixed phrases: *to be brutally honest*, *to tell you the truth*, *between you and me*. You *take something with a pinch of salt* when you don't completely believe it, say something *to put it mildly* when you could say it much more strongly, and *give someone the benefit of the doubt* when you decide to believe them although you're not sure.

L.e: To be brutally honest, the food was awful. To tell you the truth, I've never liked opera. Between you and me, I think he's leaving. Take what he says with a pinch of salt. The meeting was, to put it mildly, a disaster. I'll give him the benefit of the doubt this time.

L.p: Common polite responses include *don't mention it* (a reply to thanks), *I wouldn't dream of it* (I would never do that) and *it's the least I can do*. You invite guests to *make themselves at home*. When you can't check something yourself, you *take someone's word for it*.

L.e: 'Thanks for the lift.' 'Don't mention it.' 'Can I pay for the coffee?' 'I wouldn't dream of it!' After everything you've done, it's the least I can do. Come in and make yourself at home. 'The film's brilliant.' 'I'll take your word for it.'

units.sub: make a commitment, give a straight answer, miss the point

L.p: In a discussion you *raise an issue* (introduce it), *address an issue* (deal with it), *take a stance* (state a clear opinion) and *make a valid point* (a fair one). When the other person is right about something, you *concede the point*. A debate can be lively, heated or balanced.

L.e: Several parents raised the issue of school meals. The report fails to address the issue of cost. The party has taken a firm stance on immigration. You make a valid point about the timing. I'll concede the point about money, but not about time.

L.x: She *made a valid point* (not *did a valid point*) about the budget.

L.p: Politicians are asked to *make a commitment* (promise to do something), *honour a commitment* (keep it) and *give a straight answer* (a direct, honest one). Instead, they may *dodge the question* or *hedge their bets* (avoid committing themselves). A completely reliable promise is a *cast-iron guarantee*.

L.e: The government has made a commitment to build more homes. Will they honour their commitment? Why can't you give me a straight answer? The minister dodged the question about tax rises. Investors are hedging their bets until after the election. Nobody can give a cast-iron guarantee that it won't flood.

L.p: Someone who *misses the point* doesn't understand the most important thing. A good question gets to *the heart of the matter*. A discussion that makes no progress *goes round in circles*, and a remark that is not relevant is *beside the point*.

L.e: You're missing the point – it's not about the money. Her question got straight to the heart of the matter. We've been going round in circles for an hour. Whether he meant it or not is beside the point.

units.sub: nasty shock, take exception to, suffer at the hands of

L.p: Bad news can come as *a nasty shock*, *a rude awakening* (a sudden realisation that things are worse than you thought) or *a bolt from the blue* (something completely unexpected). You can be *badly shaken* or *taken aback* (very surprised). When something bad follows something else bad, it *adds insult to injury*.

L.e: The bill came as a nasty shock. Her first week at work was a rude awakening. The news of his resignation was a bolt from the blue. We were badly shaken by the accident. I was so taken aback that I didn't know what to say. Then, to add insult to injury, it started to rain.

L.x: The bill *came as a nasty shock* (not *came like a nasty shock*).

L.p: You *take exception to* something when you object to it strongly, and *take offence* at a remark that hurts you. People *bear a grudge* (keep feeling angry about a past wrong) and *vent their anger* (express it). Something that annoys you *gets on your nerves* (informal).

L.e: The headteacher took exception to my tone. I hope you won't take offence at what I'm about to say. He still bears a grudge against his old boss. Fans vented their anger on social media. His constant whistling gets on my nerves.

L.p: People *suffer at the hands of* others when they are badly treated by them, and *suffer in silence* when they don't complain. Someone with no patience or strength left is *at the end of their tether*, and someone in deep unhappiness is *in the depths of despair*.

L.e: Many prisoners suffered terribly at the hands of the guards. For years she suffered in silence. By Friday, I was at the end of my tether. After losing his job, he was in the depths of despair.

units.O: Describe a difficult or upsetting experience and how you felt during it. Use at least eight collocations from this unit.

units.sub: sense of achievement, state of euphoria, derive pleasure from

L.p: You *derive pleasure from* something (formal) or *take delight in* it, and informally you *get a kick out of* it. People can be *in high spirits* (cheerful and lively) or in a *state of euphoria* (extremely happy and excited). Something wonderful can *make your day* or *lift your spirits*.

L.e: She derives great pleasure from her garden. My nephew takes delight in teasing his sisters. The fans were in high spirits before the final. After the result, the whole town was in a state of euphoria. Your letter really made my day. A walk by the sea always lifts my spirits.

L.x: She *derives pleasure from* (not *derives pleasure of*) teaching young children.

L.p: Doing something difficult gives you *a sense of achievement* or *a sense of fulfilment*. After years of effort, you *reap the rewards*. A great success can be *a dream come true*, and the best thing someone has ever done is their *crowning achievement*.

L.e: Finishing the course gave me a real sense of achievement. Nursing brings her a deep sense of fulfilment. After years of training, she is reaping the rewards. Winning the cup was a dream come true. The bridge was the architect's crowning achievement.

L.p: Positive feelings also include calm and relief. *Peace of mind* is freedom from worry. You *count your blessings* when you remember the good things you have, and you *look on the bright side* when you see the good in a bad situation.

L.e: Insurance gives you peace of mind when you travel. We still have our health, so let's count our blessings. Try to look on the bright side – at least nobody was hurt.
